justification: I independently ran `node tools/run-code.mjs src/content/articles/oop-design/composition-over-inheritance.md` from PowerShell: PASS, blocks=13, executed=7, exactly matching the writer's claim. Fabrication check: I fetched all four Microsoft Learn pages myself. The inheritance page states verbatim 'A derived class can have only one direct base class' and 'A class can implement multiple interfaces even though it can derive from only a single direct base class' — both claims [[1]] and the :::dotnet callout represent this accurately. The CS1721 page's exact message is "Class 'class' cannot have multiple base classes: 'class_1' and 'class_2'" — the article's quoted diagnostic ('Class \'Wyvern\' cannot have multiple base classes...') matches the real error shape, and citation [[2]] is accurate. The exceptions page states 'an exception is an object that inherits from the System.Exception class', matching the article's claim [[4]] that .NET requires every thrown object to inherit from Exception. The ArgumentOutOfRangeException API page's Inheritance list confirms Object -> Exception -> SystemException -> ArgumentException -> ArgumentOutOfRangeException exactly as claimed at [[5]]. The GoF 'favor object composition over class inheritance' line [[3]] is one of the most widely and reliably documented sentences in software engineering literature; the article cites it by chapter (1, 'Inheritance versus Composition') rather than a page number, matching the brief's rule for books that cannot be reopened to verify a page. All 5 sources in front matter are cited inline at least once (no padded bibliography, unlike a past finding on a sibling pillar's article). No invented statistics, no asserted experience ('developers usually...', 'in production...' — none found), no unscoped absolute claims of the kind the pilot lessons warned about (checked every only/always/never/every/entire instance; each is scoped to this article's own code and reasoning, not a sweeping claim about the language or the world). Originality: the assigned shape for this article in CONTENT_PLAN.md is 'D' (bug narrative: fragile hierarchy -> break -> fragile fix -> composition refactor -> when inheritance is still right), and the body follows exactly that arc with its own invented content — a dungeon-game Enemy/Goblin/Archer/FlyingGoblin/Wyvern hierarchy, a genuine CS1721 compiler error from trying `Wyvern : Archer, FlyingGoblin`, a shipped hand-copied CrossTile override, and a specific silent regression (an added Gas hazard that the Wyvern's stale copy never picks up) that a reader can watch fail in the second run block. I compared this against Wikipedia's own composition-over-inheritance article (GameObject/Player/Cloud/Building/Trap with Visible/Solid/Movable traits — same genre (a game), completely different classes, and no bug-narrative arc at all) and confirmed via Strategy-pattern research that 'extract the independently-varying behavior into an interface and inject it via the constructor' is the textbook-canonical solution shape for this exact problem (it is, unavoidably, structurally close to Head First Design Patterns' famous Duck/FlyBehavior/QuackBehavior example and to GoF's own Strategy pattern) — but that shape is shared by virtually every correct treatment of this topic and is not evidence of copying; what is original here is the scenario, the specific compiler error, the specific regression bug, and the M-times-A-versus-M-plus-A class-count exercise, none of which echo any known toy example (Rectangle/Square, Bird/Penguin, Shape/Animal) or the Duck example's specifics. Filler/ad-code: none found; no ad code, no consent/analytics code, no keyword stuffing, no generic intro (opens directly with the domain and the ticket that breaks it) or summary-of-headings outro (closes on a runnable exercise, not a recap). Toolchain statement ('on this machine, .NET 10.0.401 on Windows 11, x64, ran each one...') sits at line 42, immediately before the first real code block at line 44, not in the opening paragraph — correct placement per the brief. Structure variety against the only sibling, four-pillars-of-oop.md: that article uses shape Q (10 of 16 headings are questions: 'What is encapsulation really protecting?', 'How does polymorphism work at run time?'); this article's six H2s are all narrative statements ('The hierarchy before this week's ticket', 'A monster that needs two things at once', 'Why the duplication wasn't bad luck') with zero question headings and zero boilerplate Introduction/Conclusion/Key-takeaways headings — genuinely different shapes, matching their different CONTENT_PLAN assignments, not a templated repeat. Exercise variety: three exercises, each a different named form from the editorial brief's list — 'Does a cast change the answer?' is predict-the-output/reasoning (decide before running, then verify), 'Add a third movement without touching a line above it' is extend-the-code, and 'How many classes does each design need?' is prove-it (derive M vs M+A algebraically). None show output or a working program outside the collapsed :::solution block, so none give away the answer, and none is titled 'Exercises' as a single terminal section — they are placed mid-article at the point each naturally lands, which is exactly what the brief's 'vary the ending' and 'do not give away exercises' lessons ask for, and improves on a finding a sibling pillar's article (sql-joins) got dinged for in its own round 1. The 'when inheritance is still the right call' section is genuine and even-handed rather than composition-always-wins: it picks .NET's real ArgumentOutOfRangeException -> ArgumentException -> SystemException -> Exception chain, runs code that catches ArgumentException to show the payoff, and gives two concrete, checked reasons inheritance is exactly right there (exceptions vary along exactly one axis, and every thrown object is required by the runtime to derive from System.Exception, so there is no composition alternative to reach for) rather than a token concession sentence. The decision not to invoke the Liskov substitution principle is explicit and documented, not just an absence: docs/crosslinks/oop-design/composition-over-inheritance.md states 'This article deliberately does not invoke LSP: the Wyvern bug is a fragile-base-class duplication bug, not a substitutability violation (every reference to Wyvern, however typed, keeps working — the returned behavior is just wrong), so citing LSP here would misapply it.' That reasoning is correct — nothing in the Wyvern example fails a substitutability check, callers holding any reference type still get a working, type-correct object, they just get stale numbers — and choosing not to reach for a nearby, prestigious-sounding citation that does not actually fit is exactly the intellectual honesty the brief's fabrication rule rewards; the article also never uses the term 'diamond inheritance' for the CS1721 scenario, which is similarly careful, since C#'s single-base-class rule sidesteps the classic diamond-ambiguity question rather than resolving it. Why not higher: a ', not X' contrast construction — the exact stylistic tic flagged as the sole real weakness in this pillar's other article's round-1 review — recurs here too (6 instances: 'not fumes', 'not to a chain of classes you extend', 'not base classes it extends', 'not two', 'not classes it extends', 'not a class'), and a near-identical 'Two things worth naming here' / 'Two things hold here' framing device opens two different paragraphs. Each instance individually carries real content rather than being filler, but the same tic recurring across consecutive articles in one pillar is precisely the kind of cross-article repetition an AdSense low-value-content reviewer is trained to notice, so it is worth trimming before it becomes this writer's signature move. No other major issues found.
